title: AgenticOS: open-source AI teammates for your company
excerpt: The self-hosted agent layer: build, run and govern AI agents on your own infrastructure. Chat, apps, a real browser, 4,700+ MCP servers and an API, with budgets, approvals and a recorded run. Apache-2.0, built on Pydantic AI by Vstorm.

Open sourceSelf-hosted · Apache-2.0 · built on Pydantic AI

Put AI to work
across your company.

The open-source agent layer for shared agents, company knowledge and automation, on infrastructure you control.

Free to run yourself under Apache-2.0. Rolled out by Vstorm when you want help.

Works with the models you already use:

AgenticOS gives every team AI teammates: agents that work with files, run code, browse the web and use your company’s tools and knowledge. Built in a browser, shared with colleagues, run on servers you own.

In pilots today

Their names stay theirs until they choose to share them.

Manufacturing · Austria

An industrial group is piloting it across its companies, with each company’s data kept apart.

Engineering · Norway

A consultancy runs it on its own servers, for its own team and for a client.

Marketing

An agency is planning its client work around a team of agents built on it.

AI teammates

Agents with a name, a job and a place on the team.

Each one has its own instructions, tools, knowledge and budget, and colleagues reach it in chat, in Slack or from the API. These six work in the demo organization.

Chief of Staff

Hands parts of a task to colleagues and writes up the brief.

  • Subagents
  • Planning

New · Projects

Your team and your agents, in one live room.

A project gives everyone the same files, instructions and a shared computer for the agents. Invite your colleagues and work the way a team works: see who is here, watch an agent's answer as it is written, reply to anyone and bring any tool in with an @.

Y Combinator put “multiplayer AI” in its Fall 2026 Requests for Startups.

Claude Code and Codex, on your team.

Any agent can hand software work to Claude Code or Codex. They work on the agent's own private computer, on the subscription you already pay for, and report every step under the answer like a colleague would.

Your experts, multiplied

Your best people’s judgment, in agents you own.

Growing a company used to mean hiring more experienced people. Here their procedures become skills, their standing facts become context, and every agent works from both. Change a rule once and every agent that reads it answers with the new one.

How it works

From a brief to the boardroom, in seven steps.

One agent, from its first sentence to a dashboard the board opens: built, taught, connected to your tools, asked in the chat and in Slack, put on a schedule and shared.

Ask in the chat, pick the agent with @

Mention an agent, drop in a file and watch every step it takes. A slash runs a command: summarize, explain, regenerate, or one your team wrote.

An animated walk-through of the console: Build: Name it, write its instructions in plain language, switch on the tools it needs and publish a version. Teach: Drop in a handbook. It is parsed, split and indexed on your own servers, and every answer cites the page it came from. Connect: Pick HubSpot, Notion or any of 4,700+ MCP servers, sign in once, and choose which tools the agent may call. Tools that change data can ask first. Chat: Mention an agent, drop in a file and watch every step it takes. A slash runs a command: summarize, explain, regenerate, or one your team wrote. Slack: Mention it in Slack, Mattermost or Telegram. It replies in the thread, with the access of the person who asked. Automate: A routine starts it every Monday, on a new GitHub issue, a Gmail message or a webhook, and keeps the dashboard current. Share: The dashboard gets a stable link and versions. Choose who opens it; every update keeps the link.

FAQ

What teams ask before they start.

Licence, local models, control, sign-in and what it takes to run.

Is AgenticOS free for commercial use?

Yes. It is licensed under Apache-2.0, which allows commercial use, modification and private deployment. You pay for the infrastructure you run it on and for the model providers and services you choose.

Is AgenticOS a product or a service?

Both. It is an open-source product you can install and run yourself, and Vstorm tailors it to your processes, data and integrations when you want help. Either way the code, the data and the infrastructure stay yours.

Can Vstorm roll it out for us, and what does that cost?

Yes. Vstorm, the team that builds AgenticOS, maps your processes, builds the agents inside your environment and hands the system over to your team, or maintains it for you. You pay for implementation and tailoring: no subscription, no seat count and no long-term commitment. A first call is 15 or 30 minutes and free of charge.

Do we need engineers to use it?

Not to build agents: instructions, tools and knowledge are set up in the browser by the people who know the work. You need someone to operate the deployment, and engineers only when you want a capability that does not exist yet, which they add in typed Python.

Can several people work with the same agents at once?

Yes. A project gives a team the same files, instructions and sandbox, and its chats are shared: everyone sees who is in the room, watches an agent's answer as it is written, replies to any message and brings in another agent, tool or document with an @. Each message carries its author's name, and each person keeps their own permissions.

Can it use the AI subscription we already pay for?

Yes. A person can sign in with ChatGPT once and run agents on that plan through Codex instead of a metered API key, and the coding agent can run Claude Code or Codex on a subscription. Budgets still count every run. A subscription belongs to one person, so for agents the whole company uses, an organization API key is the better fit. If you would rather not depend on any vendor's plan, the same agents run on your own models through Ollama, vLLM or any OpenAI-compatible server, on infrastructure you own.

Can it run with local models only?

Yes. Configure Ollama, LiteLLM or an OpenAI-compatible server such as vLLM or LM Studio, use local embedding models through Ollama, and parse documents with PyMuPDF or LiteParse. Check each destination you configure: self-hosting the console alone does not make every model, parser or tool local.

How does it keep agents under control?

Monthly budgets per agent and per organization are checked before each model request. Sensitive tools wait for a person’s approval. Optional guardrails redact secrets and personal data, and every run is recorded with its agent version, tools, tokens and cost.

Which sign-in methods and roles does it support?

Email and password with magic links, Google, OIDC single sign-on (Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, Auth0, Authentik), LDAP and Kerberos. Six built-in roles combine with department groups and per-resource sharing. MFA comes from your identity provider; there is no native MFA, SAML or SCIM yet.

How is it different from ChatGPT Enterprise, Copilot Studio or n8n?

AgenticOS runs on your infrastructure with any of 28 model providers and has no seat or credit fee of its own. It builds agents for the organization, published to chat, websites and APIs, rather than assistant seats for individual employees. Compared with n8n it starts from the agent rather than a workflow canvas, and many teams use both.

What does it take to run?

A host with 4 vCPU and 8 GB of RAM, Docker Compose and access to a model provider. A server that size typically costs $10 to $50 a month at a cloud provider, and the cost does not grow with the number of people. Models are billed by the provider you choose, or run on a subscription you already pay for. Plan for someone to operate the deployment and for subject experts who maintain the instructions and documents.
